strengths: The paper tackles a meaningful visual analogy editing problem where text prompts are often insufficient, and the proposed LoRWeB architecture is a sensible and technically sound way to specialize a diffusion editor at inference time via a learned basis of LoRA adapters and an analogy-conditioned router.

The empirical evidence is fairly broad: comparisons are made against single-LoRA and recent visual analogy baselines, with qualitative examples, automated metrics, VLM-based pairwise judgments, a small human study, and several ablations over basis size, rank, routing activation, encoder layout, and encoder backbone.

The method is practically attractive because it avoids per-example test-time optimization or training many separate LoRAs, while preserving the ability to compose transformations dynamically. The use of extended attention for the full analogy triplet and CLIP only for routing is a coherent design choice.

The ablations provide useful evidence that the gains are not simply due to parameter count: larger rank or more adapters do not monotonically improve performance, and the single high-rank LoRA remains weaker on the reported metrics.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with enough implementation detail in the appendix to understand the main training setup.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is the main concern. The custom test set is generated using Flux.1-Kontext and community Flux LoRAs, while the proposed method is also built on Flux.1-Kontext. This may bias the benchmark toward the base model and the style of transformations it can already represent, weakening claims about broad generalization to genuinely unseen visual analogies.

The human study is relatively small: 33 users over 45 image pairs, and cases where no method succeeded are filtered out. This makes the preference results supportive but not fully decisive, especially for claims of state-of-the-art generalization.

The VLM evaluation is useful but should be treated cautiously. Gemma-3 agreement with humans is reported as 66.7%, below user-user agreement, and the paper relies heavily on VLM scores and pairwise VLM win rates. More robust human evaluation or task-specific manual scoring would strengthen the case.

The comparison fairness is not fully transparent. Some baselines are based on Flux.1-Dev or prior architectures, while LoRWeB uses Flux.1-Kontext; it is unclear whether all baselines receive comparable prompts, conditioning layouts, resolutions, and inference tuning. Since the gains over the rank-128 LoRA are modest in some metrics, these details matter.

The novelty is moderate rather than transformative. Learned LoRA mixtures, routing, and adapter bases have precedent, and the paper’s main contribution is adapting this idea effectively to visual analogies. This is valuable, but the conceptual leap is somewhat incremental.

The limitations section is brief. It acknowledges difficulty with tasks far from the training corpus but does not deeply analyze failure modes, compute/memory overhead, sensitivity to prompts, possible leakage from generated evaluation data, or societal/IP issues around imitating named styles and community LoRAs.

Reproducibility is not fully established from the manuscript alone: it says code and data are on the project website, but the review copy does not provide enough detail about the released Relation252k subset issue, exact baseline implementations, or full evaluation splits to independently reproduce the reported results.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and useful problem: example-driven visual analogy editing, where text prompts alone are often insufficient to specify fine-grained transformations.

The proposed LoRWeB architecture is simple and technically plausible: a learned basis of LoRA adapters with an encoder/router that composes a task-specific adapter from the analogy triplet. This is a reasonable extension of recent observations about interpolatable LoRA weight spaces.

The paper includes comparisons to several relevant visual analogy/editing baselines, ablations over basis size, rank, normalization, and encoder choice, plus both VLM-based and human preference evaluations.
Qualitative results suggest that the method can sometimes preserve the input image while transferring style, object additions, or appearance changes better than the shown baselines.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence does not convincingly support the strong state-of-the-art and generalization claims. The main gains over the strongest single-LoRA baseline are modest in several metrics: for example, VLM edit accuracy improves only from 5.70 to 5.94 and CLIP directional similarity from 0.20 to 0.21, while the pairwise VLM win rate versus LoRA r=128 is only 57.9%. This looks like an incremental improvement rather than a decisive advance.

The evaluation set construction appears potentially biased toward the proposed setup. The custom set is generated using Flux.1-Kontext and community Flux LoRAs, then filtered to remove prompts where Flux.1-Kontext fails. Since the proposed method is built directly on Flux.1-Kontext and a LoRA-composition mechanism, this risks favoring LoRWeB over baselines and weakens the out-of-distribution generalization claim.

The baseline comparison is not fully controlled. The paper states that LoRWeB and the single-LoRA baseline use Flux.1-Kontext, while RelationAdapter, VisualCloze, and EditTransfer are based on Flux.1-Dev. Differences in backbone, conditioning interface, prompts, and implementation details may explain part of the observed performance gap.

The user study is too small and underspecified to carry much weight: 33 users over 45 image pairs, with cases filtered out when no method succeeded. This filtering could substantially bias the preference results, and the paper does not clearly report per-baseline sample counts, confidence/significance tests beyond Wilson intervals, or whether the filtering was applied identically across methods.

The VLM evaluation is over-relied upon. Gemma-3 scores are treated as central quantitative evidence, but the reported human-VLM agreement is only 66.7%, below user-user agreement of 74.2%. The paper’s statement that this is 89.9% evaluation consistency is not very convincing as validation of the metric.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate the claimed mechanism. Some variants with fewer basis elements or different ranks outperform the full model on particular pairwise comparisons or CLIP metrics, while the paper still concludes that a large basis is important. The evidence for the specific design choices is therefore mixed.

The method’s originality is moderate. Dynamic routing over multiple LoRA experts is a natural mixture-of-adapters idea, and the paper does not provide much theoretical or empirical analysis showing that the learned basis spans meaningful transformation primitives rather than acting as a larger parameterization.

Important reproducibility details are incomplete. The Relation252k train split is described as not fully public, the custom evaluation set depends on LLM-generated prompts, Unsplash images, and HuggingFace LoRAs, and the exact release status of code/data is only vaguely stated as being on a project website.

The paper has several presentation issues and typos, including inconsistent method naming in the supplement and misspellings in figures/captions. These are not fatal alone, but they add to the impression that the submission needs tightening.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically useful visual analogy editing setting, where users specify transformations through image examples rather than text alone. This is a meaningful direction for controllable image generation, especially for edits that are hard to verbalize precisely.

The proposed LoRWeB architecture is technically sensible: a learned basis of LoRA adapters with an encoder-based router provides a clear middle ground between a single global adapter and expensive per-task/test-time LoRA optimization. The method is simple, well motivated, and compatible with strong diffusion/flow editing backbones.

The experimental section is fairly comprehensive for an Algorithms/General contribution. The authors compare against several recent visual analogy baselines, include a capacity-matched single-LoRA baseline, report both automatic and pairwise VLM metrics, and add a human preference study.

The ablations are useful and directly probe the main design choices, including basis size/rank, softmax vs. tanh mixing, 2x2 encoder input vs. separate image encodings, and CLIP vs. SigLIP2 encoders. These support the claim that the basis structure and router design matter beyond merely adding parameters.

Qualitative results are strong and show appealing generalization across style transfer, object/material changes, background edits, and localized additions. The examples also suggest that the model uses the visual reference pair rather than relying only on the text prompt.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than dramatic. The main idea combines known ingredients: LoRA mixtures/bases, router-style mixture selection, and visual analogy conditioning. The paper makes a convincing engineering contribution, but the conceptual leap over mixture-of-LoRA and adapter-routing literature is somewhat incremental.

The quantitative advantage is positive but not uniformly large. For example, LoRWeB improves edit accuracy and pairwise preference, but the single LoRA baseline has comparable or better preservation/LPIPS in some metrics, and RelationAdapter is very close in VLM edit accuracy. The strongest evidence is the preference evaluation rather than a decisive metric sweep.

The evaluation relies heavily on a custom validation set generated with LLM prompts, Flux.1-Kontext, and community LoRAs. This is reasonable for probing unseen transformations, but it raises concerns about benchmark reproducibility, possible generator-specific bias, and whether the benchmark over-rewards transformations that are naturally well represented by the same ecosystem of models and adapters.

The human study is helpful but limited: 33 users and 45 image pairs, with cases where no method succeeded filtered out. This filtering can make the comparison cleaner, but it may also obscure absolute failure rates and makes it harder to judge robustness on the full task distribution.

The paper would benefit from deeper analysis of when the learned LoRA basis fails. The discussion acknowledges difficulty with transformations far from the training corpus, but the empirical treatment of failure modes, routing behavior, basis specialization, and out-of-distribution limits is fairly light.

Some comparisons could be more diagnostic. Since the method is motivated partly as an alternative to generated task-specific LoRAs/hypernetworks and test-time LoRA optimization, stronger comparisons or controlled approximations of these alternatives would clarify how much of the gain comes from the learned basis versus the underlying Flux.1-Kontext conditioning and prompt/reference-image setup.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: visual analogy editing by example, which is practically useful when transformations are hard to specify in text.

The proposed LoRWeB architecture is technically sensible: a learned basis of LoRA adapters with an input-conditioned router is a natural way to increase task-specific flexibility without expensive test-time optimization.
The method is efficient relative to per-sample optimization baselines, with reported inference overhead of only about 3.1% over a single rank-128 LoRA.

The experimental section is fairly broad, comparing against a capacity-matched Flux.1-Kontext LoRA and several recent visual analogy/edit-transfer baselines, with additional appendix comparisons to DIA, DIA-Kontext, and PairEdit.

Ablations are useful and directly probe rank/basis size, activation choice, encoder input layout, encoder backbone, and prompt dependence. The prompt/reference-pair analyses help support the claim that the model uses the analogy images rather than only the text prompt.
The paper includes a human preference study and checks VLM-human agreement, which strengthens the evaluation beyond LPIPS and CLIP directional similarity.
Limitations are stated honestly, including dependence on relatively clean reference pairs, failures on out-of-distribution transformations, small-detail edits, and multi-component transformations.
weaknesses: The empirical gains over the strongest simple baselines are sometimes modest. In Table S3, RelationAdapter has nearly identical VLM edit accuracy to LoRWeB, while the single rank-128 LoRA has better preservation and LPIPS. The main advantage is clearer in pairwise preference and qualitative examples, but the quantitative case is not uniformly strong.

The evaluation set is partly generated using Flux.1-Kontext and community Flux LoRAs, while the proposed method is also built on Flux.1-Kontext. This may bias the benchmark toward transformations and image statistics that the base model and its LoRA ecosystem already handle well.

The task remains text-guided visual analogy editing rather than purely visual analogy completion. The method follows baselines in using prompts, but the reliance on aligned prompts makes it harder to isolate how much transformation understanding comes from the reference pair versus text guidance.

The custom validation set construction involves LLM-generated prompts, manual filtering of prompts where Flux fails, generated analogy pairs, and selected category/aspect-ratio matches. These choices are reasonable but create potential selection bias and make reproducibility dependent on details that may be hard to exactly replicate.

The human study is useful but limited: 33 users over 45 image pairs, with cases where no method succeeded filtered out. This may overstate preference differences on the harder cases that matter most for generalization.

The novelty is moderate rather than fundamental. Mixture/routing of LoRA adapters is an established idea, and the main contribution is adapting it effectively to visual analogies with a learned basis; the paper would be stronger with deeper analysis of what the basis learns or whether routing corresponds to interpretable transformation modes.

The method inherits practical constraints of visual analogy datasets: it assumes access to a reasonably clean before/after exemplar pair, and appendix examples show that identity/background changes in the exemplar pair can corrupt the output.

Some claims about spanning the visual analogy space are stronger than the evidence supports. The experiments demonstrate improved empirical flexibility, but not that the learned LoRA basis meaningfully spans a broad transformation space beyond the tested prompt/generated benchmark distribution.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and timely problem: example-based visual analogy editing, where text prompts alone are often insufficient to specify detailed transformations.

The proposed LoRWeB architecture is simple and plausible: a learned basis of LoRA adapters with an input-conditioned router, applied to a strong conditional flow/editing backbone. This is a reasonable engineering idea and is clearly explained.

The manuscript includes several useful comparisons and ablations, including capacity changes, routing activation, encoder input layout, alternative image encoders, comparisons to per-sample optimization methods, and some failure cases.

Qualitative examples suggest that the method can sometimes preserve the target image better than prior analogy/edit-transfer baselines while capturing style, object additions, and background/appearance changes.

The authors make an effort to evaluate beyond CLIP/LPIPS by including VLM-based scoring and a human preference study, and they discuss practical limitations such as the need for well-aligned reference pairs.
weaknesses: The central empirical gain over the most relevant baseline, a capacity-matched Flux.1-Kontext LoRA, is modest. In Table 1/S3, LoRWeB improves VLM edit accuracy only from 5.70 to 5.94, has slightly worse preservation than the single LoRA, worse LPIPS, nearly identical CLIP directional score, and only a 57.9% pairwise VLM win rate. This makes the main claim that the LoRA basis substantially improves generalization insufficiently convincing.

The novelty is incremental. Dynamic mixtures/routing of LoRAs and LoRA composition are well-established ideas, and the paper’s adaptation to visual analogies is useful but not conceptually deep enough without stronger empirical evidence.

The evaluation is heavily dependent on synthetic/custom data generated using Flux.1-Kontext and community LoRAs, while the method itself is built on Flux.1-Kontext. This raises concerns that the benchmark may favor the chosen backbone and may not reflect robust real-world analogy editing.

The VLM evaluation is not fully convincing as primary evidence. Gemma-3 scores and pairwise preferences may be biased by image quality or prompt priors, and the reported human-VLM agreement is only moderate. The paper reports user-user agreement as 74.2% and user-VLM agreement as 66.7%, which does not strongly validate replacing human judgment with VLM scores.

The human study is small and potentially biased: 33 users and 45 image pairs, with filtering of cases where no method succeeded. This filtering could remove difficult examples and inflate the apparent preference for the proposed method.

The comparison setup is not always clean. Some baselines use different underlying backbones or expensive per-sample optimization, while the strongest same-backbone single-LoRA baseline is close to LoRWeB. The paper would need a more rigorous apples-to-apples comparison to justify the added architectural complexity.

The method still relies on text prompts in addition to analogy images. Although the authors include prompt ablations, the results do not fully isolate how much of the edit is learned from the visual pair versus recovered from the textual instruction and the strong pretrained editor.

Reproducibility is limited by dependence on Relation252K splits that are stated as not fully publicly available, custom generated evaluation data, community LoRAs, and a large proprietary/rapidly evolving editing backbone. Code is promised but not present in the manuscript.

Several limitations are important for deployment: the approach assumes fairly clean before/after reference pairs, struggles with small changes and multi-component edits, and can fail on transformations outside the training distribution. These limitations directly affect the claimed generality of visual analogy editing.
The writing and presentation contain noticeable typos and inconsistencies, including misspellings in figures and text, which do not invalidate the work but reduce confidence in polish and care.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely visual analogy editing problem, where example-based control can express transformations that are hard to specify textually. The motivation is clear and the proposed LoRWeB formulation is a sensible Algorithms/General contribution.

The central idea of learning a basis of LoRA adapters with an input-dependent router is technically clean, efficient, and well matched to the task. It improves over a single fixed LoRA without requiring expensive test-time optimization or training thousands of independent adapters.

The experimental section is fairly comprehensive: the paper compares against several recent analogy/editing baselines, a capacity-matched single-LoRA baseline, DIA/DIA-Kontext, and PairEdit; it also includes qualitative results, automated metrics, pairwise VLM evaluation, user study results, efficiency analysis, and ablations over rank, basis size, activation, and encoder choices.

The authors make a good effort to test whether the method actually uses the reference analogy pair rather than merely following the text prompt, including reduced-prompt experiments, different reference-pair examples, and discussion of prompt/image misalignment.

The paper is generally well written and reproducible at the method level, with concrete hyperparameters, optimizer/training details, model choices, evaluation prompts, and dataset construction details. The limitations section is meaningful and acknowledges failures on out-of-distribution transformations, subtle edits, multi-component edits, and the practical difficulty of obtaining clean before/after reference pairs.
weaknesses: The novelty is solid but somewhat incremental: the paper combines known ingredients, LoRA mixtures/bases, CLIP-style routing, and image-grid conditioning on a strong Flux.1-Kontext backbone. The contribution is more an effective architectural adaptation than a fundamentally new learning principle.

The evaluation set is partly synthetic and generated using Flux.1-Kontext or community Flux LoRAs, while the method itself is based on Flux.1-Kontext. This raises a possible evaluation-bias concern: the test distribution may favor methods built around the same model family and editing behavior, even though the authors include some checks with non-Flux reference images.

Some baseline comparisons are hard to interpret because several baselines use different backbones, require different prompts, or are adapted by the authors rather than used in their native setting. The capacity-matched Flux LoRA is the cleanest comparison, and the gains over it are positive but not uniformly large across all metrics.

The VLM-based evaluation is useful but still imperfect. The reported user study is relatively small, with 33 users over 45 image pairs, and the VLM-human agreement is meaningfully below inter-human agreement. Stronger human evaluation over more tasks would make the empirical case more convincing.

The method still depends on textual prompts and relatively clean analogy pairs. The paper shows that LoRWeB can use image evidence beyond the prompt, but it is not a fully prompt-free visual analogy method, and behavior under ambiguous, conflicting, or real-world noisy reference pairs remains only lightly explored.

The paper would benefit from deeper analysis of the learned LoRA basis: for example, whether basis elements specialize semantically, whether routing weights cluster by transformation type, and how stable the learned basis is across random seeds or training datasets. This would strengthen the claim that the method spans a meaningful visual analogy space rather than simply acting as a larger conditional adapter.
